newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's army still wields clout from the wings.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's army still wields clout from the wings.

text.p: Pakistan's military played a main role in sacking former prime minister Benazir Bhutto, although it kept a low profile during an abrupt transfer of power, analysts and diplomats said on Wednesday.

The army put on a modest display of force in the early hours on Tuesday when President Farooq Leghari dissolved the National Assembly, dismissed Bhutto, named a caretaker government and called fresh elections for next February.

An army spokesman, who asked not to be named, said just two companies, or 200 to 300 soldiers, took control of sensitive installations in the capital Islamabad. Similar numbers were deployed in provincial capitals Lahore and Karachi.
"It was just a precautionary measure," he said.

But analysts and diplomats said there was no doubt the armed forces, particularly army chief of staff Jehangir Karamat, had thrown their weight behind Leghari, who cited corruption, nepotism and extra-judicial killings as reasons for Bhutto's dismissal.
Leghari grounded his decision to dismiss the prime minister in the eigth amendment to Pakistan's constitution, adopted in 1985.

The controversial amendment empowers the president to dissolve National Assembly if "a situation has arisen in which the Government of the Federation cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution".
"The way and manner in which he (Leghari) acted spotlighted his power and status more as a Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces," the Nation newspaper said.
"He would thus skilfully spare the armed forces from the unpalatable task of direct intervention in civilian affairs and its inevitable grave consequences."

The third and last period of martial law in Pakistan's 49-year history ended the same year the amendment was passed. In the 11 years since, presidents have used the authority to oust four governments, including two headed by Bhutto.

"The army has been involved in all four dissolutions," said a senior defence analyst who asked not to be named. "Yesterday's dissolution has the full consensus of the army. It is a kind of constitutional coup."
The persistent influence of the military was reflected in a reluctance among many defence experts to speak on the record.
The army has ruled Pakistan for nearly half of its 49 years, exercising power through three periods of martial law starting in 1958 and ending in 1985.
The amendment which enabled the president to sack Bhutto has allowed the army to wield influence from the sidelines.
"The army did not have to send a greater force yesterday morning as there was no challenge," the defence analyst said. "There is no built-in civilian force which would resist a takeover."

Bhutto opposed Karamat's appointment as army chief of staff earlier this year and supported a rival general, analysts said. But Leghari prevailed. "The legacy of this disagreement has now had its impact," one analyst said.
A diplomat said there had been continuous meetings between Leghari and army officers over the past month. "There emerged a consensus between the president and the army."
While the military has ruled Pakistan for much of its history, it is growing reluctant to take direct control.

"Over the past 10 years there has been a distinct shift," a diplomat said. "When Bhutto first came to power in 1988, the army was still very prickly about defending its political role. But more recently it has kept a very, very low profile."
"The military thinks democracy has to be given a chance and the army should not be back in direct power," an analyst said.
But the military's political clout has not dissipated.
"The army is widely perceived as being the only organising unit in Pakistan, as a national unifying force," one diplomat said.
"If political parties developed more fully and there were smoother elections, the army might be able to step aside. But I don't see that happening for 10 years at least."
